Day 9 since the college fest.
Sumit, 6:02 am: Good morning to the most beautiful mind I have ever met.
Parul, 7:40 am: Morning! Sorry, just woke up. Class at 9.
Sumit, 7:41 am: Skip it? I want to hear your voice.
Sumit, 7:45 am: You took long to reply. Did I say something wrong?
Parul, 7:46 am: No no, I was asleep.
Sumit, 7:46 am: I've never felt like this. It's like we were meant to find each other.
Parul, 7:50 am: It's only been nine days, haha. But honestly, nobody has ever talked to me like this.
Sumit, 7:51 am: Nine days, nine years, same thing when it's fate. Let's plan a trip together next month.
Parul, 7:53 am: A trip? I don't even know your middle name, or what you're like when you're grumpy.
Sumit, 7:53 am: You'll learn everything. Just don't pull away from me.
Parul typed "okay", deleted it, then typed it again.

qa.a: Nine days had passed since the college fest.

qa.a: Parul feels flattered and specially chosen by Sumit's attention, even while the joke about not knowing a middle name shows a small doubt about the speed.

qa.q: What could Parul do at the moment of typing "okay" about the trip?
qa.a: Parul could pause instead of agreeing, say a trip is too soon, keep going to class, and see whether Sumit stays kind when the pace slows.

qa.q: What would change if Sumit answered the middle-name joke with patience and ordinary details?
qa.a: Parul would get room to know a real person instead of a story about fate, and the pressure to reply fast and agree to a trip would ease.

grounding: A young adult, nine days after meeting someone, is flooded with early-morning messages and talk of fate and feels uniquely chosen, while the rush leaves no time to learn who Sumit really is.

The phone in Rukmini's lap buzzed again as the bus rattled past the sugarcane fields. Twelve messages from Tushar since breakfast. A photo of the temple fair where they had met eleven days ago, with a line: the day my life began. Another: No one will ever understand you like I do.
Rukmini pressed the phone to her chest. At home she was the quiet middle daughter, rarely asked what she thought. Tushar asked her everything.
"He wants me to meet his mother on Sunday," she told Minakshi, her bench-mate at the typing class.
Minakshi's eyebrows rose. "What does he do on weekdays?"
Rukmini opened her mouth and found she did not know. She knew his favourite song and that he called her his destiny, but not where he worked or who his friends were. She read the newest message twice, then left it unanswered until the bus stopped.

qa.q: How many messages had Tushar sent since breakfast?
qa.a: Tushar had sent twelve messages since breakfast.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini press the phone to her chest?
qa.a: She felt treasured and noticed; at home she was rarely asked what she thought, so Tushar's constant questions made her feel chosen.

qa.q: What could Rukmini do after realising she did not know what Tushar does on weekdays?
qa.a: She could hold off on meeting his mother on Sunday, ask plain questions about his work and friends, and give herself time to learn who he is.

qa.q: How does Minakshi see the rush from the outside?
qa.a: Minakshi seems puzzled that a family meeting is planned when basic facts are missing, and the raised eyebrows and simple question show gentle concern rather than judgement.

grounding: A young woman in a small town, swept up by messages about destiny from a man she met eleven days earlier, realises she knows little about his actual life.

Last March my roommate Ojas met someone at a dance workshop, and by the next Saturday I barely recognised our flat. Our Sunday grocery run? Cancelled. The group trip to the waterfall? Ojas stayed back to wait for a call. Every dinner story was about Kiran: Kiran's poems, Kiran saying they were soulmates, Kiran wanting Ojas to move in by summer.
I'm Reena, and I'm bad at hard talks. I wrote three versions of what to say and deleted them all. In the end I just said, over chai, "I've noticed you've stopped doing the things that were yours. I might be wrong. I'm not going to lecture. I just miss you."
Ojas went quiet, then said I didn't understand real love. I said maybe not, and that the Sunday grocery run would still happen at ten.
Three Sundays later, Ojas showed up at ten, eyes puffy, holding the cloth bags.

Sit, Nirmala. Your Urmila Nani will tell you about the summer she was twenty.
A boy called Devesh from the next lane began sending letters through my brother every single day. Beautiful letters. By the second week he wrote that we should marry before the rains. My heart was racing, I won't lie. But my Amma had taught me one thing: fast rivers carry mud.
So I wrote back only this: "I like your letters. I want to know you slowly. I will still go to my sewing class, and to Saroj's house on Thursdays."
Then I waited to see what he would do. His next letter came four days later, not one. It said: "Take all the time you need. Tell me what you are stitching."
That letter, beta, is the reason I said yes a year later. Your Nana still asks me what I am stitching.

qa.a: He wrote that they should marry before the rains.

qa.q: How was young Urmila feeling when the marriage letter came?

qa.a: She said she liked him but kept her sewing class and Thursdays at Saroj's house, which slowed things without ending them and let her see how Devesh treated a gentle no.

qa.q: How might Devesh have felt when her slow reply arrived?
qa.a: He may have felt a little disappointed, but his warm letter asking what she was stitching shows he respected her pace and was curious about her life.

Yamini had three exams in five days and a phone that would not stop glowing. Rashmi, whom she had met at a college hackathon barely three weeks earlier, had booked two bus seats to the hills for Friday. "Surprise! Our first trip," the message said, followed by a row of hearts.

In February, Javier had filled Hiroshi's tiny Lisbon flat with yellow tulips and left notes on the bathroom mirror: You are the best thing that ever happened to me. By June the notes were gone.
Now Hiroshi stood at the stove at eleven at night, stirring the bean stew Javier used to love, because yesterday Javier had called the flat "depressing" and Hiroshi "boring lately". He had already changed his shirt twice.
The key turned. Javier walked past the table, glanced at the pot and said, "I ate."
Hiroshi ate alone, scrolling back through old messages from February. Good morning, beautiful. Can't wait to see you. He read them the way people reread a favourite book, hoping the ending might change. Then he opened a message to his sister in Kyoto, typed "Is it normal to feel like I'm auditioning in my own home?", and for the first time, pressed send.

qa.q: What did Javier fill the flat with in February?
qa.a: Javier filled the flat with yellow tulips.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi hope for when he reread the February messages?
qa.a: He was hoping the warm Javier of February would come back, the way someone rereads a favourite book wishing the ending might change.

qa.q: Why was pressing send to his sister a turning point for Hiroshi?
qa.a: Naming the feeling to someone outside let him check what was happening; the gap between February's tulips and June's "I ate" is the pattern, and support can help him stop auditioning for warmth.

At fifteen I had one best friend, Ravi. The school cricket final fell on the same Sunday as his cousin's engagement. I wanted him there so badly it hurt. But did I say that? Wasim, you check your phone every time your mother calls, even mid-shift. Your Damini Aunty has nursed on this ward for thirty years. Listen to something from when I was twenty.
My Ammi raised four of us alone, and she never let me forget it. If I wanted to join the college trip, she would say, "Go. Who am I? Only the one who sold her bangles for your fees." Then she would not eat dinner. So I stayed. I missed the trip, the drama club, my best friend's wedding.

Elif had not spoken to Rafael all morning, and the Porto flat felt smaller because of it. At lunch she finally set down her fork. "Three years we lived here. I covered your rent when you lost the café job. And now you just leave me for Berlin."
Rafael felt the familiar tug in his chest. He made himself ask the question slowly, in his head: did I actually wrong her? He had told her in March, two months early, as their flat agreement said. He had paid back the café months by summer. The answer was no.
"I'm grateful for that rent, truly," he said. "And I'm still going. I'll help you find someone good for my room, and I'll call on Sundays."
Elif's eyes filled. "It won't be the same."
"No," he said gently. "It won't. I'll miss this too."

On the class trip, at the dhaba, I laughed when Kunal read out your diary page, and I said, "Give it here, let's see more." When you brought it up last week, I told you it never happened. Three girls in my class sat behind me. One day they poured ink on my geography map and wrote a nasty word across it. "Arre, it was a joke. Can't you take a joke?" By the next week they were telling everyone it never happened, that I had spilled the ink myself.

By lunch Usha was wondering if she had heard wrong.
Mausi pulled the shutter halfway down against the rain and listened without interrupting. Then she said, "Pooja told me about that dinner on the phone. You heard it right, and it's okay that it hurt. I'll speak to your Mummy gently this weekend."
Usha let out a breath she felt she had held all day. Mausi made tea and helped with two maths problems while the rain slowed.

qa.q: What exam did Usha have the next morning?
qa.a: Usha had her maths exam the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Usha let out a breath she felt she had held all day?
qa.a: She felt relief, because Mausi confirmed she had heard right and that her hurt made sense, easing a day of doubt.

qa.q: Why was getting off the bus to see Rashmi Mausi a wise choice, despite the rain and the exam?
qa.a: Talking to a trusted adult outside the dinner table let Usha check her memory against someone else's, which helped her trust herself again.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had said "I heard it too" instead of "Let it go"?
qa.a: Usha would not have spent the day doubting herself; one person at home confirming it would have kept her trust in her own memory steady.

grounding: A girl whose mother denies a hurtful remark at dinner begins to doubt herself, and a trusted aunt outside the situation confirms what she heard.

passage:
Paulo checked the calendar on his phone for the third time. There it was: Thursday, 6 p.m., café shift, and underneath, Told Jin Monday. He had even written that.
Still, when he got home, Jin was sitting in the dark. "You never said you were working. You just disappear and expect me to guess."
"I told you on Monday, remember? At the laundromat."
"That didn't happen. You always do this. You rewrite things so you look good."
Paulo opened his mouth, then closed it. Last week it had been the concert tickets, and before that the rent money. Each time Jin was certain, and each time Paulo ended up saying sorry.
"Sorry," he said now. "Maybe I forgot to say."
Later, washing dishes in their Melbourne flat, he noticed he had started writing everything down, and still didn't trust it. He wasn't sure anymore whether he was a forgetful person, or had only been told he was.

qa.q: What had Paulo written under the Thursday shift in his calendar?
qa.a: He had written "Told Jin Monday" under the café shift.

qa.q: What is Paulo feeling as he washes the dishes?
qa.a: He feels confused and less sure of himself, no longer knowing whether he is truly forgetful or has only been told he is.

qa.q: What could Paulo do the next time his note and Jin's version clash?
qa.a: He could trust his written note, calmly say he remembers it differently without apologising, and check his experience with someone he trusts outside the flat.

qa.q: What would change if Jin said "I don't remember that, maybe I missed it" instead?
qa.a: The disagreement would be about a missed message, not about Paulo's mind, and he would not need to apologise for something that was not wrong.

grounding: A young man repeatedly told he rewrites events starts apologising for things he did not do and doubts even his own written notes.

passage:
"Ishita, you uploaded the wrong data file again," Tarun said loudly across the chemistry lab, so the whole bench heard.
Ishita's cheeks burned. She was almost sure she had uploaded the file he sent her at midnight. Almost. All semester Tarun had told her she misheard the meeting time, that she overreacted when he took credit for her graphs, that she "always gets emotional". Somewhere along the way, almost sure had become the most she ever felt.
"Sorry, sorry, my fault," she said, before checking anything.
Professor Rao looked up from the fume hood. "Let's see the shared folder." The file history showed Tarun had sent that file at 12:04 a.m.
Tarun shrugged. "Whatever, small thing."
Ishita stared at the screen. She had apologised for his mistake, again, without a second's thought. On the walk back to the hostel she counted how many times she had said sorry that week, and stopped at eleven.

qa.q: What did the file history show?
qa.a: The file history showed Tarun had sent that file at 12:04 a.m.

qa.q: What does Ishita's instant "Sorry, sorry, my fault" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels anxious and ashamed, no longer trusting her own memory, and rushes to take the blame even when almost sure she isn't at fault.

qa.q: What small step could Ishita take the next time Tarun blames her?
qa.a: She could pause and check the record before apologising, keep her own notes of shared work, and talk it over with Professor Rao or someone she trusts.

qa.q: How might Professor Rao see what happened at the bench?
qa.a: Professor Rao seems to want facts rather than accusations and, after seeing the file history, may realise Ishita has been taking blame that was not hers.

grounding: A student told all semester that she mishears and overreacts apologises by reflex for Tarun's mistake and notices how far her confidence has shrunk.
